I was born white, and brought up in white culture, second generation Western European. The values imparted in me were: if I tried hard, paid attention, and applied myself, I could become an independent adult who would be able to engage in a lifestyle that I enjoyed. No one promised me wealth, fame, or power. I was raised to believe that I, alone, would be responsible for myself. My family was poor. My father worked, and provided the best he could. I was never led to believe that our financial status was anyone’s fault. There were times when my father would switch jobs and we would be a little better off, and times when he would be laid off, and we would collectively deal with it, without complaint. The material goods that my family owned were respected and cared for, so they would last.

I was taught, by example, that I shouldn't steal, cheat, or commit crimes. The consequences were obvious, and I was shown examples of what happens when individuals have a disregard for laws and rules. This doesn't mean that I didn't have rebellious phases, or that I didn't learn my own lessons, but my transgressions, by today's standards, were minor. Education came first, and if I screwed up at school, I would hear about from my parents. I was more worried about disappointing them, than I was about getting punished. My parents celebrated my successes and they coached me through my failures. My parents were far from perfect, but I learned to respect their intentions.

I was never taught to hate other cultures, on the contrary, I was taught to respect and admire the aspects of those cultures that I could learn from and even emulate to become better. I learned tremendous respect for Japanese discipline, European dedication to tradition, African American musical and culinary creativity, the tremendous resilience of the Irish. I think the main difference is that I never was forced to try to integrate into other cultures. To respect them was enough, I didn’t have to live them. There was no reason to feel inferior/superior. I was also cautioned that there were lifestyles that could destroy my future, and to avoid those lifestyles.

I wasn’t a high honors student, but I often did a little better than average. I went to college. I worked jobs – shit jobs – but I worked hard. I found that if I put in a good effort, people would eventually recognize it, and I would become more valuable and companies would depend on me, leading to promotion/monetary increase.

My current life is a balance of working hard, and then using my free time to do the things that I enjoy. Working offers me the financial means to do things that I like. My life pursuits aren’t extravagant, but I get a lot of satisfaction from them. I am not looking for more. I have children, and I am imparting the same idealism and values into them. I am also allowing them the freedom to decide who they want to be, and not be defined by their gender, career, or culture.

I see so many stereotypes about white people on the internet. No one handed me a life. No one subsidized my career, or schooling. I earned everything that I have, and I have a feeling of accomplishment because of it.

I encourage anyone from different cultural backgrounds to tell your story. I think we can cut through the bullshit stereotypes and really see how each culture has it's own version of contributing positively to society.
